figures.caption: Figure 1: Fraction of points in knn(q) which hash collide with q and c respectively. Measured by applying 1000 random functions from Hrp to 100 random queries, over the MirFlickr Dino2 dataset. It is possible for q to collide with only a small fraction of knn(q), whereas this is not possible for an element c ∈ Φ.
Figure 2: Comparison of query algorithm for: abstract LSH-based ANN model (above) and our modification (below).

Figure 3: Recall results for an RP-Forest and MQ-Forest consisting of y trees. Note that the degree of vertical difference between the two curves represents improvement; lower is better. For example, MirFlickr can be searched at a recall of approximately 75% in 96 trees for RP-Forest, and approximately 43 for MQ-Forest whilst reducing the number of distance calculations.
Figure 4: Distance computations for an RP-Forest and MQ-Forest consisting of y trees.
Figure 5: RP-Forest and MQ-Forest: Recall vs Queries Per Second. Note the log-scale y axis. Searching for k = 20 near neighbours.
Figure 6: Fraction of points in knn(q) which collide with q (left column) and c (right column). Measured using 1000 randomly drawn hash binary functions and 100 queries.
Figure 7: Average value of κ from estimating c via a random selection of 100 elements the m nearest neighbours.
Figure 8: Aggregated off-diagonal covariance values when applying a large number of binary hash functions to ⟨c⟩ (blue) and q (orange) as instances of u. Measured over 100 random queries.
Figure 9: Rate of change of the candidate set after trees in an RP-Forest are searched. k = 100.
Figure 10: The distributions of co-ordinate 0 of c− q, ⟨ĉ⟩ − q, and ⟨ĉ⟩ − c over 5000 queries.
Figure 11: The distributions of co-ordinate 0 of c and ⟨ĉ⟩ over 5000 queries.
Figure 12: Empirical observations vs theoretical model of the distribution of co-ordinate 0 if ⟨ĉ⟩−c over 5000 separate queries.
